title: Love Poetry and the Wasf
lead: The Song of Songs belongs to a family of love poetry known from Egypt, Mesopotamia and later Greece and Arabia. Its descriptive praise of the body, the wasf (an Arabic term), its use of 'sister' and 'brother' for lovers, and its gardens and animals have close parallels in the Egyptian songs of the New Kingdom and in Syrian wedding songs recorded in the 1800s. These parallels show the Song's genre and do not, by themselves, show its date or its meaning.

sections.b: About fifty Egyptian love songs survive on papyri and pottery pieces from the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties (about 1300–1100 BC), among them Papyrus Chester Beatty I, the Turin papyrus, Papyrus Harris 500 and the Cairo Love Songs. In them a girl and a boy, who call each other 'sister' and 'brother', speak of love as sickness, praise one another's hair and eyes, and use gardens, birds and perfumed oils as images. Michael Fox (1985) found many close points of likeness with the Song. Because the Egyptian songs are some centuries earlier and in another language, scholars do not think the Song copied them; they show a shared tradition of the ancient Near East.

sections.h: Mesopotamian songs and the sacred marriage
sections.b: Sumerian songs of Dumuzi and Inanna tell the courtship of a shepherd god and a goddess of love, with milk, apples, gardens and a woman who opens a door to her lover. Some scholars (Pope, Jacobsen) have drawn the Song close to this tradition, and a few have read it as a descendant of the cult. Most do not, because the Song contains no gods or rites; the likenesses are in the language of love, which the Song shares with its neighbors.

sections.b: A wasf is a praise-song that lists the beloved's body part by part. The Song has four: 4:1–7, 5:10–16, 6:4–10 and 7:1–9. Syrian wedding customs of the 1800s, recorded by J. G. Wetzstein and used by Franz Delitzsch, included such songs sung to a bride in the 'king's week', and Delitzsch built a reading of the Song on them. Scholars no longer treat the Song as a record of those customs, but the form is real.
